text.title: Cognitive Walkthrough: Process Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for running the walkthrough as a session: the four prerequisites that must exist before evaluators arrive, panel composition, the no-design-debate ground rule, the step budget that forces the streamlined variant, keeping per-evaluator answers un-merged, and prioritising by earliest blocking step.

rule.statement: `prerequisites` MUST contain all four inputs before the session is scheduled: (1) a user description including prior knowledge, (2) one specific task, (3) the correct action sequence for that task, (4) an interface representation showing the state after each action. A session missing any one is cancelled, not run in reduced form.

rationale.source: Wharton, Rieman, Lewis & Polson, "The Cognitive Walkthrough Method: A Practitioner's Guide" (1994) — prerequisites section

rule.rationale: Each missing input is silently supplied by the evaluators from memory during the session, and each evaluator supplies a different one. The disagreements then read as findings about the interface when they are disagreements about which interface was being inspected.

rule.statement: `evaluators` MUST list 2-4 named people with roles, and at least one MUST NOT have worked on the design under test. A solo walkthrough is recorded as an inspection draft, not as a walkthrough result.

rationale.source: Wharton et al. (1994); Spencer, "The Streamlined Cognitive Walkthrough Method" (CHI 2000)

rule.rationale: A designer cannot simulate ignorance of labels they chose — they answer Q2/Q3 from knowledge of where the control is, so their yes carries no information. Above four people, step-by-step discussion outruns the session and the later steps get waved through.

rule.statement: Ground rules recorded with the session MUST forbid defending the design and forbid designing fixes while walking the steps; proposed fixes go to a parking list and are worked only in the synthesis phase. Check: during-session `issues` rows have `fix` empty; `prioritized_findings` is written after the last step.

rationale.source: Spencer, "The Streamlined Cognitive Walkthrough Method" (CHI 2000) — social constraints in development teams

rule.rationale: Spencer's field observation was that defensiveness and premature fix-hunting, not the method, killed walkthroughs in real teams: one design argument eats the time budget for a dozen steps, and the group compensates by answering the remaining steps yes.

rule.statement: The session MUST declare its variant and fit the step count to it: full four-question walkthrough for tasks up to roughly 15-20 atomic steps in a 60-90 minute session; longer tasks either split at sub-goal boundaries into separate sessions or switch to the streamlined two-question variant ("will the user know what to do here?" and "will they know they did the right thing?"), recorded in the artefact.
rule.rationale: The four-question form costs several minutes per step with a group. When the task is longer than the budget, teams do not stop — they accelerate, and the tell is a form where the final third is uniformly yes. Choosing the cheaper variant up front keeps the whole task covered at honest depth.

rule.statement: `evaluation_forms` MUST retain each evaluator's own Q1..Q4 answers per step, and `issues[].evaluator_consensus` MUST record the split (e.g. unanimous, 2-of-3) rather than overwriting with a group verdict. Disagreements MUST NOT be resolved by the most senior person's answer.

rationale.source: Wharton et al. (1994) group procedure; inspection-method agreement literature

rule.rationale: A split answer is the strongest available signal that the step is genuinely ambiguous — three competent evaluators simulating the same persona diverged. Collapsing to a majority verdict deletes exactly the data with the highest hit rate for real first-use failures.

rule.statement: Every issue MUST carry the step index and which question failed. Routing is fixed by the tag: Q1 → goal/mental-model or wrong entry point, Q2 → visibility and affordance, Q3 → label, wording and iconography, Q4 → feedback and state change. An untagged issue is not accepted into `prioritized_findings`.

rationale.source: Polson, Lewis, Rieman & Wharton (IJMMS, 1992) — question-to-breakdown mapping

rule.rationale: The question that failed determines which change can possibly fix it. Untagged, a Q3 label failure gets answered with a tooltip or onboarding, which leaves the mismatched label in place and adds a second thing to read.

rule.statement: `prioritized_findings` MUST be ordered so that blockers at the earliest step index come first, and MUST state explicitly that findings after the first blocker are conditional on that blocker being fixed. Re-walk the tail after fixing an early blocker rather than shipping the tail fixes as verified.

rationale.source: Wharton et al. (1994) — sequential assumption that each prior step succeeded

rule.rationale: Each step is evaluated assuming the previous ones worked. A blocker at step 2 makes every later finding a statement about a state no current user reaches, so fixing them first buys nothing measurable and the early blocker survives another release.
